title: Roman doctors: three senses of ‘venial’—from cause, event, or nature
source_text: I. Observant Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae peccatum veniale triplici modo dici, vel a causa, vel ab eventu, vel ex ipsa natura & ratione peccati. Peccatum veniale a causa vocant peccatum quod ex ignorantia, vel ex infirmitate committitur. Quod genus peccati non dicitur veniale, ut distinguatur contra quodcunque mortale; sed contra peccatum mortale ex malitia. Tametsi enim peccata ex ignorantia, vel ex infirmitate saepe sint mere mortalia, tamen dicuntur omnia venialia, quia est in eis aliquid imminuens culpae pravitatem, & ratione cujus is qui peccavit vicinior est indulgentiae. De quo genere peccati loquitur Apostolus, quum ait, Qui blasphemus, & contumeliosus, & persecutor fui; sed misericordiam consecutus sum, quia ignorans feci in incredulitate. 1 Tim. 1.
pass_a_gloss: The doctors of the Roman Church observe that venial sin is said in a threefold way: either from the cause, or from the event, or from the very nature and reason of the sin. Sin venial from the cause they call a sin that is committed from ignorance or from infirmity. Which kind of sin is not called venial so as to be distinguished against every mortal sin, but against mortal sin from malice. For although sins from ignorance or from infirmity are often merely mortal, yet they are all called venial, because there is in them something diminishing the wickedness of the fault, and by reason of which he who has sinned is nearer to indulgence. Of which kind of sin the Apostle speaks when he says that he was a blasphemer and injurious and a persecutor, but obtained mercy because he did it ignorantly in unbelief (1 Tim. 1).
pass_b_english: Roman School usage splits ‘venial’ three ways: by cause, by event, and by the sin’s own nature.
Sins of ignorance or weakness can still be mortal, yet are called venial insofar as something softens guilt and draws nearer to pardon.
